 Appeals court allows lawyer to challenge police, govt seizure of ASNB accounts
 Appeals court allows lawyer to challenge police, govt seizure of ASNB accounts
 29-Oct-2026, 12:57 29 Oct 2026, 12:57 FMT Reporters Share Court of Appeal rules that Rosli Dahlan’s case against the authorities cannot fairly be characterised as frivolous or vexatious.
 Justice Choo Kah Sing said Rosli Dahlan demonstrated a prima facie arguable case that the freeze orders might have been affected by mala fide, collateral purpose, irrationality or abuse of power. 
 PETALING JAYA : The Court of Appeal today unanimously allowed lawyer Rosli Dahlan’s appeal against the High Court’s refusal to grant him leave to commence judicial review proceedings challenging the seizure of four of his Amanah Saham Nasional Bhd (ASNB) accounts by the police and government. 
 A three-member bench chaired by Justice Choo Kah Sing, sitting with Justices Nadzarin Wok Nordin and Latifah Tahar, set aside the High Court’s Aug 14, 2024 decision and granted Rosli leave to pursue his judicial review of the seizure orders dated Jan 12, 2024.
 Rosli had named former attorney-general Ahmad Terrirudin Salleh as the first of nine defendants.
 Delivering the unanimous decision, Choo held that Rosli had demonstrated a prima facie arguable case that the seizure orders may have been affected by mala fide (bad faith), collateral purpose, irrationality or abuse of power.
 The Court of Appeal disagreed with the High Court’s finding that Rosli’s case was insufficiently pleaded against the seizure orders issued under Section 50 of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing, Anti-Restricted Activity Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001.
 The Court of Appeal held that the High Court had erred in determining contested issues at the preliminary leave stage. Choo emphasised that the wrong test had been used at the leave stage.
 “This court is of the considered view that the learned High Court judge approached the matter at a level of scrutiny more appropriate for a substantive hearing than for a leave application.
 “The question is not whether mala fide has been proven, but whether the pleaded allegations disclose an arguable basis for asserting mala fide.
 “Viewed in its entirety, the appellant’s case cannot fairly be characterised as frivolous or vexatious,” he said.
 The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and remitted the matter to the High Court for a full hearing and determination of the substantive merits of Rosli’s challenge against the issuance of the seizure orders.
 Rosli was represented by lawyers Chetan Jethwani, Harvinderjit Singh, Amiratu Al Amirat, Ho Yu Fei and Shavitta Devi, while senior federal counsel Normastura Ayub and Zulkifli Sulaiman appeared for the police and government.
